newsitem.title: USA: Texas gas production flat despite rise in drilling.
newsitem.headline: Texas gas production flat despite rise in drilling.

text.p: Texas natural gas production levels are expected to remain steady in the coming years despite stepped-up exploration in the state, analysts said.

Texas natural gas production has hovered around 5.6 trillion cubic feet (tcf) a year while the number of gas well completions has climbed steadily over the past five years, according to state regulators.
But increased spending on exploration and production has yet to translate into forecasts of higher production levels from state fields, analysts said.

"Most forecasts that I'm aware of see Texas production remaining fairly stable in the next few years," said Ron Kitchens, director of gas services with the Texas Railroad Commission. "(But) without new spending, we would see a significant decline in the total production rates."

Texas gas production in 1996 rose to 5.8 tcf, but is on pace through the first quarter of 1997 to fall back to the 5.6 tcf level of recent years, according to statistics from the commission, which regulates statewide oil and gas production.
"The additional investment in (natural gas) exploration has basically brought on enough new production to compensate for the decline in old production," Kitchens said.

While Texas gas production has remained relatively flat, natural gas well completions have risen steadily to 4,060 last year, the highest level in ten years and nearly equal for the first time to the number of oil wells completed in the state.
"Drilling wells is like building houses for builders, that's your cash-flow generation," said Michelle Foss, director of the CBA Energy Institute at the University of Houston.
Estimates released late last year raised recoverable natural gas reserves in Texas to 427 trillion cubic feet (tcf) from 249 tcf, sparking renewed interest in the potential of state fields.

Analysts expect state gas production to remain steady despite several major projects announced this year, including Conoco's decision in May to invest $1 billion over five years to develop more than 2.7 trillion cubic feet of reserves in its newly acquired Lobo Trend acreage in south Texas.
